questions.q: Four companies since 2023. What is the interviewer actually worried about?
questions.a: A cost, not a character flaw. Companies split departures into two kinds. Regretted attrition is the people they wanted to keep and lost. Unregretted is everybody else. Only the first is tracked as a problem. Replacing a good engineer costs a recruiting process, an empty seat through a notice period, and months of ramp. Managers carry that number into their own reviews. So the worry is that they pay to hire you and you leave before it pays back. What knowing this buys is the right register. Answer the cost. Saying you are loyal addresses nothing they measure.
questions.flag: Hearing it as an accusation. It is a risk calculation, and treating it as one keeps the conversation useful instead of defensive.

questions.q: What does ramp time have to do with it?
questions.a: It is the thing being priced. Ramp time is the period between starting and the point where you produce more than you consume in other people's time. For a senior engineer it is commonly three to six months, spent consuming code review, onboarding and context. A twelve-month stay pays back some of that. A seven-month stay pays back very little. What naming it buys is an objection that can actually be answered, because an abstract worry about commitment has no reply. You can shorten it in the answer by saying what you would need in week one and what you could ship in month one.
questions.flag: Promising to stay a long time. It is unfalsifiable and everybody says it. A concrete first-month plan is the version they can act on.

questions.q: When do you raise your notice period?
questions.a: In the first conversation, unprompted. A notice period is the contractual gap between resigning and leaving. In India it is frequently sixty or ninety days, against two weeks in much of the world, and it is enforceable rather than a courtesy. That makes it a real constraint on a hiring timeline. It also explains gaps between roles on your own page. What raising it early buys is that it stays scheduling. Discovered at offer stage it looks like something you were managing. There is no version where waiting helps you, and several where it costs you the role.
questions.flag: Waiting to be asked. Recruiters plan around start dates, and a surprise at the end is the most expensive moment to deliver one.

teach.title: The story these four roles actually tell

questions.q: If your current employer counter-offered, would you take it?
questions.a: A counter-offer is a raise your current employer makes after you resign, specifically to stop you leaving. It is common enough that recruiters plan for it. The statistic they all quote is that most people who accept one leave anyway within a year. They are asking because a candidate who takes one costs them an entire completed process. What understanding that buys is knowing this is not idle curiosity. Answer directly. If money were the issue you would have raised money. If it is not, say what the issue is, and say a raise does not change it. Vagueness here reads exactly like the answer they fear.
questions.flag: “I would consider it.” True of everyone and fatal here, because it tells them the offer they are about to make may be used as leverage.

questions.q: What does a background check actually verify?
questions.a: A formal verification of the factual claims on your résumé, run by the employer or a third-party firm. In practice that means employment dates, job titles, and in India frequently salary, confirmed against payroll records rather than your account of them. What knowing the scope buys is clarity about where precision is mandatory and where description is fine. Dates are where quiet discrepancies live. Make the months on the page match the payslips exactly. Rounding a departure to the nearest quarter tidies the résumé and fails a check, and the check happens after you have accepted.
questions.flag: Smoothing a gap by stretching a date. It buys nothing, and it is the one category of problem that surfaces after the offer.

questions.q: One of these was fixed-term. Does that count as a short stay?
questions.a: No, and it is your job to say so on the page. A fixed-term or agency engagement has an agreed end built into it from the first day. Permanent employment does not. They look identical in a list of dates and they are different relationships. A contract that ran its full length and ended on schedule is a contract completing. What one label buys is an entire line of questioning removed, at no cost to anything. An unlabelled twelve-month entry reads to a stranger as a twelve-month resignation. That is a misunderstanding you handed them for free.
questions.flag: Explaining it in the room. By then they have already read the dates and drawn a conclusion. Fix it on the page.

questions.q: Why is your title not useful evidence here?
questions.a: Because titles are not comparable across companies. Inside a company, roles sit at internal grades that determine scope, expectations and pay range. That grade is the real currency and it is normally not public. Titles are set by convention and inflation, so “Senior” at one company may be two grades below “Senior” at another. Four employers means four conventions with no shared scale. What knowing this buys is understanding why your titles are not doing the work you assumed. So describe scope instead. What you owned, who depended on it, what you decided without asking. Scope compares across companies. Senior does not.
questions.flag: Arguing that a title was under-levelled. It sounds like grievance, and the scope description makes the same point without the complaint.

teach.title: The story these four roles actually tell

questions.q: Somebody asks about the job history. What are they really asking?
questions.a: Whether this happens again. A hire takes months to be worth what it costs, so a short tenure is a loss somebody has to explain internally. It is a risk estimate rather than a judgement, which means the answer has to lower an estimate rather than win an argument.
questions.flag: Hearing it as an accusation. That produces a defensive answer, and the defensiveness is what actually does the damage.

questions.q: What shape should the answer have?
questions.a: A fact, a reason, and what you are optimising for now. About fifteen seconds. Then stop and let them follow up if they want to. The forward half is the part that speaks to what they are actually pricing, and it is the part most people leave out.
questions.flag: Filling the silence afterwards. The pause feels long to you and normal to them, and everything said into it sounds like justification.

questions.q: “You were at Innovaccer for seven months.”
questions.a: Say the fact back plainly, give one reason about the work, and name what the move bought. On this résumé it bought a level and a platform to own, which is checkable from the titles. What you must not do is spend thirty seconds on it.
questions.flag: Any sentence about the manager or the team. It is heard as a preview of how you will describe this place.

questions.q: “And you have only been at CloudSufi nine months.”
questions.a: This one is harder, because the answer cannot be about what went wrong. It has to be about what this role offers that the current one cannot, said without criticising a job you still hold. Anything negative about a current employer is the most expensive thing you can say.
questions.flag: Explaining why the current role disappointed you. The one you are in is the one they listen to most carefully.

questions.q: “Walk me through your résumé.”
questions.a: Two minutes, chronological, one sentence per role, ending on what you are looking for. Do not pause on the transitions, because pausing marks them. The thread to carry is ownership. Prototypes, then a shipped system, then a platform owned end to end.
questions.flag: Reciting the bullets. They have read those. What they want is the connective tissue between the roles.

teach.title: The story these four roles actually tell

questions.q: Why does it have to be the same sentence every time?
questions.a: Because interviewers compare notes, and two different reasons is a much bigger problem than one short role. A reason that shifts between rounds reads as an improvised one. Writing it down and saying it until it is boring is the entire technique.
questions.flag: Tailoring the reason per interviewer. The tailoring is what gets noticed, not the reason.

teach.title: The test the reason has to pass

questions.q: What if a departure was not your decision?
questions.a: Then say so plainly and early, and the question mostly disappears. A layoff is a fact about a company rather than about you, and it is the one explanation that needs no defending. What damages people is hedging around it until it sounds like something else.
questions.flag: Dressing it up as a choice. It is checkable, it is common, and the vaguer version sounds worse than the real one.

questions.q: “Where do you see yourself in a few years?”
questions.a: The same question again, wearing a different hat. The answer that works names something that takes years and exists here. Depth in a domain, or ownership of something that grows. Anything achievable in a year is an answer that schedules your next departure.
questions.flag: Naming a title. A title is portable and says nothing about staying anywhere in particular.

questions.q: So what is the sentence?
questions.a: That one is yours, and it has to be true. A rehearsed sentence you do not believe sounds exactly like one. The scaffold is fact, reason, forward. The reason has to pass the reproduction test. Write it, then say it aloud twenty times.
questions.flag: Improvising it in the room. This is the one answer where improvisation is guaranteed to be worse than preparation.

questions.q: What if the honest reason was money?
questions.a: Then it needs a frame. Stated bare, it predicts the next move exactly. Compensation following scope is a different sentence from compensation for its own sake. If the move also came with more to own and a higher level, lead with that. It is true, and it is the part that does not recur here.
questions.flag: Making it the headline. Everyone understands it and nobody hires on it, because a larger number always exists somewhere.

questions.q: They push back on your answer.
questions.a: Repeat it, do not extend it. The temptation is to add detail, and detail is what makes it sound like a story being built. Saying the same thing again, calmly and without new material, is what a settled answer looks like.
questions.flag: Adding a second reason under pressure. Two reasons read as neither being the real one.

questions.q: Does the answer change for a recruiter?
questions.a: No, and that is the point. The recruiter writes it down and it travels. A version tuned for a screening call becomes the version the hiring manager compares against later. That is how inconsistency gets manufactured out of nothing.
questions.flag: Treating the screen as informal. It is the round where your words get transcribed most literally.

questions.q: What does the two-minute version contain?
questions.a: One sentence per role and one thread through them. Not the bullets, which they have read. Move through the transitions at the same speed as everything else, because slowing down at a short tenure is what marks it as a problem.
questions.flag: Spending longer on the short roles. Time spent is read directly as discomfort.

questions.q: Which questions are this question in disguise?
questions.a: Where do you see yourself. What are you looking for. What would make you turn down an offer. Why us. All four are asking how long you stay, and answering them consistently matters as much as the direct version does.
questions.flag: Answering these from a different frame. They are the same question and a careful interviewer is checking the answers against each other.

questions.q: “What would have kept you at the last place?”
questions.a: A sharp question, because a vague answer here undoes the earlier one. The good version names something specific and structural, and it should be the same thing your reason implied. If it is something this company has, say so, because that is the whole point of naming it.
questions.flag: Saying nothing would have. That says the decision was about leaving rather than about arriving somewhere.

questions.q: “You have breadth. Do you have depth?”
questions.a: The fair version of the concern, and the résumé answers it. The same thread runs through every role. Agents, retrieval, evaluation and the guardrails around them, across four employers and two publications. That is depth in a domain that happened to move between companies.
questions.flag: Listing technologies. The answer is that one problem area recurs, not that many tools appear.

teach.title: The story these four roles actually tell

questions.q: Is there a gap anywhere in these dates?
questions.a: No, and that is worth knowing, because it removes a whole category of question. The roles run continuously from January 2023, and the degree finished inside the first one. Saying that cleanly if asked is better than working it out live.
questions.flag: Being unsure about your own dates. Hesitating over the timeline makes a clean one sound unclean.

questions.q: What about references from a seven-month role?
questions.a: Expect the question and have a name ready. A short tenure with a willing reference is a much smaller concern than a short tenure with a shrug. Knowing who you would name, before being asked, is most of the work here.
questions.flag: Avoiding the shortest role when references come up. The omission is the thing that gets noticed.

questions.q: Should you ask them the same question back?
questions.a: Yes, and it repositions the conversation. Ask how long people stay on this team, and what the last person who left went on to do. That is a normal question from somebody evaluating a decision rather than hoping for one. It also gives you the information you need.
questions.flag: Asking it as a retort. Timing matters, and it belongs in your questions at the end rather than immediately after theirs.

questions.q: When is the question itself a signal about them?
questions.a: When it keeps coming back after a straight answer, or when it turns into a comment about loyalty. One careful pass is due diligence. Three is a place that will treat the tenure as leverage later, and noticing that is part of what you are there to do.
questions.flag: Absorbing repeated pressure as though it were fair. The interview goes both ways and this is one of the clearer signals available.

questions.q: What if the honest reason is one you would rather not give?
questions.a: Then find the part of it that is true, structural and sayable, and give that. Not a different reason, a narrower one. Inventing a reason is the failure mode, because an invented reason has no detail behind it and the second question finds the edge of it.
questions.flag: Constructing a story. Every follow-up tests it, and the effort of maintaining it shows in the delivery.

teach.title: The test the reason has to pass

questions.q: You are interviewing while employed. Does that change the tone?
questions.a: It helps, and it constrains you. A current job means you are choosing rather than needing, which is a good position. It also means nothing critical can be said about the place you are still at, because that is the most expensive sentence available.
questions.flag: Criticising a current employer. It is heard as what you will say about them in a year, and with more force than any past-employer comment.

questions.q: Two roles appear to overlap in the dates.
questions.a: Explain it in one sentence and move on, because the explanation is almost always mundane. A notice period, a start date, a final year of study. What turns it into a problem is hesitation, since an unexplained overlap invites a much worse guess than the truth.
questions.flag: Hoping nobody reads the months. Somebody in the loop reads the months.

questions.q: The interviewer is openly sceptical about the job-hopping.
questions.a: Stay level and give the same answer. Matching their temperature is the error, and so is over-apologising. If it persists past a straight answer, that is information about how this place treats leverage, and you are allowed to use it.
questions.flag: Getting defensive. The content of the answer matters far less than the fact that the answer did not rattle you.

questions.q: What if a role was always meant to be short?
questions.a: Then say so, and label it on the résumé. A fixed-term role that reads as a resignation is a self-inflicted problem. One word next to the dates removes a question that would otherwise take a minute.
questions.flag: Leaving it ambiguous. The reader's default assumption is the unfavourable one.

questions.q: You have two offers and one is likely to be short again.
questions.a: Worth weighing honestly, because the next timeline is being written now. Another short role makes every future version of this conversation harder, and the compounding is real. That is an argument for staying somewhere long enough to own an outcome, not just a task.
questions.flag: Optimising only the immediate move. The pattern is what gets priced, and each entry makes the next explanation more expensive.

questions.q: Defend the pattern.
questions.a: I would reframe it rather than defend it. Four employers is the surface. What actually happened is that each move bought more to own, and the titles moved with it. That is checkable from the résumé, and it is the only reading of the timeline that is a story.
questions.flag: Arguing that tenure does not matter. It does to them, and disputing the premise is a worse move than reframing it.

teach.title: The story these four roles actually tell

questions.q: What would you change?
questions.a: Write the sentence down and stop improvising it. Say it aloud until it is dull. And where the résumé can remove a question cheaply, label it. Every question you pre-empt is a minute spent on the work instead.
questions.flag: Treating this as less worth preparing than the technical rounds. It is asked in every single one of them.

questions.q: The reason you give for leaving has to satisfy one hard constraint. Which?
questions.a:
Say the reason out loud and ask whether it would also be true of the job you are interviewing for. If it would, you have described the next departure in your own words, and the interviewer will hear exactly that.

Keeping people out of it is a good rule too, and it is a rule about tone rather than the load-bearing constraint. Reasons outside your control are rarer than people pretend, and a structural reason about scope works fine.
options: It must be something this job cannot reproduce
It must be entirely outside your own control
It must involve nobody you worked with then
It must be flattering about the previous employer

teach.title: The test the reason has to pass

questions.q: When should a short tenure come up in the conversation?
questions.a:
Raising it yourself converts a concern they would have dug up into one you have already handled. It also removes their reason to probe, because they have the answer without having had to ask for it.

Waiting means the topic arrives as a challenge rather than as information. And leaving it to the offer stage means it surfaces when the cost of a surprise is highest for both sides.
options: Before they do, in the opening minutes
Only when they ask about it directly
At the offer stage, with the recruiter
In the follow-up note you send afterwards

questions.q: “Walk me through your résumé.”
questions.a: Lead with the thread rather than the timeline. LLM systems since the start of 2023, agents and retrieval and the evaluation around them, with two peer-reviewed papers across the same years. Then the roles in order, one sentence each, at an even pace. Research prototypes at Samsung, a shipped agentic debugger with layered validation at Innovaccer, and a platform owned end to end at CloudSufi one level up. Name the seven months yourself, in one sentence, and finish on what you are looking for now.

teach.title: The story these four roles actually tell

questions.q: “Seven months at Innovaccer. What happened?”
questions.a: Three parts and no more. The fact, said plainly with no adjectives. A reason about the work rather than about people, which has to be one this job does not reproduce. Then what the move bought, which on this résumé is a higher level and a platform to own. Then stop. The silence afterwards feels long to you and normal to them, and anything said into it sounds like justification rather than information.

questions.q: “How do I know you will not leave in six months?”
questions.a: Answer the thing being estimated rather than the thing being said. What makes a stay likely is something that takes years and exists here, so name it specifically. Then be honest about the pattern rather than disputing it, because disputing the premise is worse than reframing it. Each move bought more ownership, and the next thing I want is long enough to own an outcome rather than a task, which is not a promise about intent but a statement about what I am selecting for.

questions.q: “What are you looking for?”
questions.a: Whatever you name here has to be the same thing your leaving reason implied, and it has to be something this company visibly has. Not growth and not impact, because those exist everywhere and therefore explain nothing about staying here. Something structural about scope, ownership or the kind of problem, and ideally something that takes more than a year to get, because an answer achievable in twelve months schedules your next departure out loud.

questions.q: “What are you working on outside work?”
questions.a: Name something that exists rather than something you intend. A curriculum you are actually working through has a shape and a syllabus and can be described in a sentence, which is more than any claim about being curious can do. It also answers the depth concern indirectly, because sustained study of one area is exactly what somebody worried about breadth is listening for.
